[[File:Autographer lifelogging device.png|alt=A close up of a person's neck and upper torso, with a black rectangular sensor and camera unit attached to their shirt collar|thumb|256x256px|AI-enabled [[Wearable technology|wearable]] sensor networks may improve [[Occupational safety and health|worker safety and health]] through access to real-time, personalized data, but also presents [[psychosocial hazard]]s such as [[micromanagement]], a perception of [[surveillance]], and [[information security]] concerns.]]
The impact of [[artificial intelligence]] on workers includes both applications to improve [[Occupational safety and health|worker safety and health]], and potential [[Occupational hazard|hazards]] that must be controlled. Another use is to track productivity.

One potential application is using AI to [[Hazard elimination|eliminate hazards]] by removing humans from hazardous situations that involve risk of [[Occupational stress|stress]], [[overwork]], or [[Musculoskeletal injury|musculoskeletal injuries]].  [[Predictive analytics]] may also be used to identify conditions that may lead to hazards such as [[fatigue]], [[Repetitive strain injury|repetitive strain injuries]], or [[Chemical hazard|toxic substance exposure]], leading to earlier interventions.  Another is to streamline [[Occupational safety and health|workplace safety and health]] workflows through automating repetitive tasks, enhancing safety training programs through [[virtual reality]], or detecting and reporting [[Near miss (safety)|near misses]].

When used in the workplace, AI also presents the possibility of new hazards.  These may arise from [[machine learning]] techniques leading to unpredictable behavior and [[Inscrutable artificial intelligence|inscrutability]] in their decision-making, or from [[Computer security|cybersecurity]] and [[information privacy]] issues.  Many hazards of AI are [[Psychosocial hazard|psychosocial]] due to its potential to cause changes in work organization.  These include increased [[employee monitoring|monitoring]] leading to [[micromanagement]], algorithms unintentionally or intentionally [[Algorithmic bias|mimicking undesirable human biases]], and [[Blame in organizations|assigning blame]] for machine errors to the human operator instead.  AI may also lead to [[physical hazard]]s in the form of [[Workplace robotics safety|human–robot collisions]], and [[Human factors and ergonomics|ergonomic]] risks of control interfaces and human–machine interactions.  Hazard controls include cybersecurity and information privacy measures, communication and transparency with workers about data usage, and limitations on [[Cobot|collaborative robots]].

== Adoption by companies ==

Many technology companies have taken measures to incentivize or require the use of generative AI tools by their employees. In October 2026, [[Epic Games]] CEO [[Tim Sweeney]] announced that the company would be "moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration." [[Bloomberg News|Bloomberg]] reported that staff on a Disney collaboration were asked to finish the game using entirely AI tools, including directives such as "no more hand-written code" and art assets being "generated with full AI workflows."<ref name="bbc-epic-games-oct2026">{{Cite news |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cvj6j812dg4no |title=Fortnite-maker Epic Games confirms 'huge pivot' towards using AI |last=De Souza |first=Naomi |date=2026-10-13 |website=BBC |access-date=2026-10-15 }}</ref>

=== Token maxxing ===
'''Token maxxing''' or '''tokenmaxxing''' (also '''token maxing'''), a term that uses the [[wikt:incelosphere|incelosphere]]-related suffix ''"-maxx"''<ref name="wiredsource">{{Cite news |last=Klee |first=Miles |date=2026-02-25 |title=Everyone Speaks Incel Now |url=https://www.wired.com/story/everyone-speaks-incel-now/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260302040717/https://www.wired.com/story/everyone-speaks-incel-now/ |archive-date=2 March 2026 |access-date=2026-08-05 |work=Wired |language=en-US |issn=1059-1028}}</ref> is a metric used in an attempt to track productivity in the workplace especially for those using [[artificial intelligence]] (AI) based services. AI services charge for each token which represent units of effort expended by an AI service to solve a problem. Some believe that token consumption equates to productivity and thus can be used as a metric to monitor an employee's work.<ref name="auto2">{{Cite web |last=Keary |first=Tim |date=13 April 2026 |title=Is The Cult Of ‘Tokenmaxxing’Just Another Fad Or The New Normal? |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/timkeary/2026/04/13/is-the-cult-of-tokenmaxxingjust-another-fad-or-the-new-normal/ |access-date=2 May 2026 |website=[[Forbes]]}}</ref><ref name="auto">{{cite web | title='Tokenmaxxing' has techies debating if leaderboards tracking AI token use are a good idea | website=[[Business Insider]] | url=https://www.businessinsider.com/tokenmaxxing-ai-token-leaderboards-debate-2026-4 }}</ref><ref name="auto4">{{Cite web|url=https://www.wbur.org/onpoint/2026/04/28/tokenmaxxing-how-tech-workers-are-gamifying-their-way-to-unemployment|title=Why the tech world is ‘tokenmaxxing'|first1=Claire|last1=Donnelly|first2=Meghna|last2=Chakrabarti|date=28 April 2026|website=www.wbur.org}}</ref><ref name="auto3">{{Cite web|url=https://www.businessinsider.com/jpmorgan-disney-employees-vie-for-ai-leaderboard-status-tokenmaxxing-2026-4|title=Tell us if you're on the AI leaderboard at work — and if you support 'tokenmaxxing' to get there|first=Hayley|last=Peterson|website=Business Insider}}</ref><ref name="auto5">{{Cite web|url=https://www.wsj.com/cio-journal/why-some-companies-say-ai-tokenmaxxing-is-key-to-survival-e699a128|title=Why Some Companies Say AI ‘Tokenmaxxing’ Is Key to Survival|first=Isabelle|last=Bousquette|date=14 April 2026|website=The Wall Street Journal}}</ref>
 
Supporters believe that higher token usage indicates higher productivity and higher use of powerful AI services. Critics claim that prudent workers will maximize any metric that management wants increased to gain a workplace advantage, such as by running several AI agents in tandem, entering longer input prompts, or excessively automating tasks to maximize token consumption. To management, this higher token usage may indicate potential productivity, but in reality may cause additional token costs, worker burnout, or actually create more bloated code of lower quality. Another claim is AI service companies potentially benefit from such an emphasis on token consumption and actively encourage the trend.<ref name="forbes">{{cite news |last1=Nieva |first1=Richard |title=The ‘AI Gods’ Spending As Much As They Can On AI Tokens |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/richardnieva/2026/03/31/the-ai-gods-spending-as-much-as-they-can-on-ai-tokens/ |publisher=Forbes |date=31 March 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260331105136/https://www.forbes.com/sites/richardnieva/2026/03/31/the-ai-gods-spending-as-much-as-they-can-on-ai-tokens/ |archive-date=31 March 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web
 |title=AI cost crisis hits tech giants as employee tokenmaxxing backfires — agentic AI eats up to 1,000x more tokens than standard AI, sparks corporate pullback at Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon
 |url=https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/artificial-intelligence/ai-cost-crisis-hits-tech-giants-as-employee-tokenmaxxing-backfires-agentic-ai-eats-up-to-1000x-more-tokens-than-standard-ai-sparks-corporate-pullback-at-microsoft-meta-and-amazon
 |website=Tom's Hardware
 |access-date=28 May 2026
}}</ref>

Some developers have publicly advocated the practice. Developer Sigrid Jin, who said he used 50&nbsp;billion tokens in a single year, has argued that maximizing token consumption is the best way to understand the value of AI, advising others to spend as much on AI usage as they pay in rent to obtain a return on investment.<ref name="axios">{{Cite web |last=Mills |first=Madison |date=13 May 2026 |title=Tokenmaxxer: AI should cost as much as your rent |url=https://www.axios.com/2026/05/13/tokenmaxxer-ai-claude-code-codex |website=[[Axios (website)|Axios]] |access-date=13 May 2026}}</ref>

== Health and safety applications ==
For any potential AI health and safety application to be adopted, it requires acceptance by both managers and workers.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Jakub |first1=Fiegler-Rudol |last2=Karolina |first2=Lau |last3=Alina |first3=Mroczek |last4=Janusz |first4=Kasperczyk |date=30 January 2025 |title=Exploring Human–AI Dynamics in Enhancing Workplace Health and Safety: A Narrative Review |journal=Int. J. Environ. Res. Public Health |volume=22 |issue=2 |pages=199 |doi=10.3390/ijerph22020199 |pmid=40003424 |pmc=11855051 |doi-access=free }}</ref>  For example, worker acceptance may be diminished by concerns about [[information privacy]],<ref name="ergonomic" /> or from a lack of trust and acceptance of the new technology, which may arise from inadequate transparency or training.<ref name="risks" />{{Rp|26–28, 43–45}}  Alternatively, managers may emphasize increases in [[Productivity|economic productivity]] rather than gains in worker safety and health when implementing AI-based systems.<ref name="health" />

=== Eliminating hazardous tasks ===

AI may increase the scope of work tasks where a worker can be [[Hazard elimination|removed from a situation that carries risk]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=P N |first1=Lee |last2=M |first2=Lee |last3=A M |first3=Haq |last4=E B |first4=Longton |last5=V |first5=Wright |date=1 March 1974 |title=Periarthritis of the shoulder. Trial of treatments investigated by multivariate analysis. |journal=Ann Rheum Dis |volume=33 |issue=2 |pages=116–119 |doi=10.1136/ard.33.2.116 |pmid=4595273 |pmc=1006221 }}</ref>  In a sense, while traditional automation can replace the functions of a worker's body with a robot, AI effectively replaces the functions of their brain with a computer.  Hazards that can be avoided include stress, overwork, musculoskeletal injuries, and boredom.<ref name="benefits">{{Cite web|last=Moore|first=Phoebe V.|date=7 May 2019|title=OSH and the Future of Work: benefits and risks of artificial intelligence tools in workplaces|url=https://osha.europa.eu/en/publications/osh-and-future-work-benefits-and-risks-artificial-intelligence-tools-workplaces/view|access-date=30 July 2020|website=EU-OSHA}}</ref>{{Rp|5–7}}

This can expand the range of affected job sectors into [[White-collar worker|white-collar]] and [[Tertiary sector of the economy|service sector]] jobs such as in medicine, finance, and information technology.<ref name="labor">{{Cite journal|last1=Frank|first1=Morgan R.|last2=Autor|first2=David|last3=Bessen|first3=James E.|last4=Brynjolfsson|first4=Erik|last5=Cebrian|first5=Manuel|last6=Deming|first6=David J.|last7=Feldman|first7=Maryann|last8=Groh|first8=Matthew|last9=Lobo|first9=José|last10=Moro|first10=Esteban|last11=Wang|first11=Dashun|date=2 April 2019|title=Toward understanding the impact of artificial intelligence on labor|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|language=en|volume=116|issue=14|pages=6531–6539|doi=10.1073/pnas.1900949116|issn=0027-8424|pmc=6452673|pmid=30910965|bibcode=2019PNAS..116.6531F |doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Analytics to reduce risk ===

Machine learning is used for [[people analytics]] to make predictions about worker behavior to assist management decision-making, such as hiring and performance assessment.  These could also be used to improve worker health.  The analytics may be based on inputs such as online activities, monitoring of communications, location tracking, and [[voice analysis]] and [[Computer processing of body language|body language analysis]] of filmed interviews.  For example, [[sentiment analysis]] may be used to spot fatigue to prevent [[overwork]].<ref name="benefits" />{{Rp|3–7}}  [[Decision support system]]s have a similar ability to be used to, for example, prevent [[industrial disaster]]s or make [[disaster response]] more efficient.<ref name="implications" />

For manual [[material handling]] workers, [[predictive analytics]] and artificial intelligence may be used to reduce [[musculoskeletal injury]].  Traditional guidelines are based on statistical averages and are geared towards [[Anthropometry|anthropometrically]] typical humans.  The analysis of large amounts of data from wearable sensors may allow real-time, personalized calculation of [[Human factors and ergonomics|ergonomic]] risk and [[fatigue]] management, as well as better analysis of the risk associated with specific job roles.<ref name="ergonomic">{{Cite web|last=Gianatti|first=Toni-Louise|date=14 May 2020|title=How AI-Driven Algorithms Improve an Individual's Ergonomic Safety|url=https://ohsonline.com/articles/2020/05/14/how-aidriven-algorithms-improve-an-individuals-ergonomic-safety.aspx|access-date=30 July 2020|website=Occupational Health & Safety|language=en}}</ref>

[[Wearable technology|Wearable sensors]] may also enable earlier intervention against exposure to toxic substances than is possible with area or breathing zone testing on a periodic basis. Furthermore, the large data sets generated could improve [[workplace health surveillance]], [[Occupational risk assessment|risk assessment]], and research.<ref name="implications">{{Cite journal|last=Howard|first=John|date=1 November 2019|title=Artificial intelligence: Implications for the future of work|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/ajim.23037|journal=American Journal of Industrial Medicine|language=en|volume=62|issue=11|pages=917–926|doi=10.1002/ajim.23037|pmid=31436850|bibcode=2019AJIM...62..917H |s2cid=201275028|issn=0271-3586|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

=== Streamlining safety and health workflows ===
AI has also been used to attempt to make the [[Occupational safety and health|workplace safety and health]] workflow more efficient. One example is [[Coding (social sciences)|coding]] of [[workers' compensation]] claims, which are submitted in a prose narrative form and must manually be assigned standardized codes. AI is being investigated{{by whom|date=January 2026}} to perform this task faster, more cheaply, and with fewer errors.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Meyers|first=Alysha R.|date=1 May 2019|title=AI and Workers' Comp|url=https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/blogs/2019/ai-workerscomp.html|access-date=3 August 2020|website=NIOSH Science Blog|language=en-us}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last1=Webb|first1=Sydney|last2=Siordia|first2=Carlos|last3=Bertke|first3=Stephen|last4=Bartlett|first4=Diana|last5=Reitz|first5=Dan|date=26 February 2020|title=Artificial Intelligence Crowdsourcing Competition for Injury Surveillance|url=https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/blogs/2020/ai-crowdsourcing.html|access-date=3 August 2020|website=NIOSH Science Blog|language=en-us}}</ref>

== Hazards ==
[[File:Blackbox3D.png|thumb|320x320px|Some [[machine learning]] training methods are prone to unpredictabiliy and [[Inscrutable artificial intelligence|inscrutability]] in their decision-making, which can lead to hazards if managers or workers cannot predict or understand an AI-based system's behavior.|alt=A drawing showing a back rectangular solid labeled "blackbox", with an arrow entering labeled "input/stimulus", and an arrow exiting labeled "output/response"]]

There are several broad aspects of AI that may give rise to specific hazards.  The risks depend on implementation rather than the mere presence of AI.<ref name="benefits" />{{Rp|2–3}}

Systems using sub-symbolic AI such as [[machine learning]] may behave unpredictably and are more prone to [[Inscrutable artificial intelligence|inscrutability]] in their decision-making.  This is especially true if a situation is encountered that was not part of the AI's [[training data]]set, and is exacerbated in environments that are less structured.  Undesired behavior may also arise from flaws in the system's [[Machine perception|perception]] (arising either from within the software or from [[sensor]] degradation), [[knowledge representation and reasoning]], or from [[software bug]]s.<ref name="risks" />{{Rp|14–18}}  They may arise from improper training, such as a user applying the same algorithm to two problems that do not have the same requirements.<ref name="benefits" />{{Rp|12–13}}  Machine learning applied during the design phase may have different implications than that applied at [[Runtime (program lifecycle phase)|runtime]].  Systems using [[Symbolic artificial intelligence|symbolic AI]] are less prone to unpredictable behavior.<ref name="risks">{{Cite web|last1=Jansen|first1=Anne|last2=van der Beek|first2=Dolf|last3=Cremers|first3=Anita|last4=Neerincx|first4=Mark|last5=van Middelaar|first5=Johan|date=28 August 2018|title=Emergent risks to workplace safety: working in the same space as a cobot|url=https://publications.tno.nl/publication/34627026/je8DYe|access-date=12 August 2020|website=[[Netherlands Organisation for Applied Scientific Research]] (TNO)}}</ref>{{Rp|14–18}}

The use of AI also increases [[Computer security|cybersecurity]] risks relative to platforms that do not use AI,<ref name="risks" />{{Rp|17}} and [[information privacy]] concerns about collected data may pose a hazard to workers.<ref name="ergonomic" />

=== Psychosocial ===
[[File:Pyxis_Pharmacy_Robot_by_Nurse_Station.JPG|thumb|Introduction of new AI-enabled technologies may lead to changes in work practices that carry [[psychosocial hazard]]s such as a need for [[retraining]] or fear of [[technological unemployment]].]]
[[Psychosocial hazard]]s are those that arise from the way work is designed, organized, and managed, or its economic and social contexts, rather than arising from a physical substance or object.  They cause not only [[psychiatric]] and psychological outcomes such as [[occupational burnout]], [[anxiety disorder]]s, and depression, but they can also cause physical injury or illness such as [[cardiovascular disease]] or [[musculoskeletal injury]].<ref name="euosha">{{Cite web|last1=Brun|first1=Emmanuelle|last2=Milczarek|first2=Malgorzata|date=2007|title=Expert forecast on emerging psychosocial risks related to occupational safety and health|url=https://osha.europa.eu/en/tools-and-publications/publications/reports/7807118|access-date=3 September 2015|publisher=European Agency for Safety and Health at Work|archive-date=23 December 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181223235709/https://osha.europa.eu/en/tools-and-publications/publications/reports/7807118|url-status=dead}}</ref>  Many hazards of AI are psychosocial in nature due to its potential to cause changes in work organization, in terms of increasing complexity and interaction between different organizational factors.  However, psychosocial risks are often overlooked by designers of advanced manufacturing systems.<ref name="health">{{Cite journal|last1=Badri|first1=Adel|last2=Boudreau-Trudel|first2=Bryan|last3=Souissi|first3=Ahmed Saâdeddine|date=1 November 2018|title=Occupational health and safety in the industry 4.0 era: A cause for major concern?|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0925753517315035|journal=Safety Science|language=en|volume=109|pages=403–411|doi=10.1016/j.ssci.2018.06.012|hdl=10654/44028 |s2cid=115901369 |hdl-access=free|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Einola and Khoreva explore how different organizational groups perceive and interact with AI technologies.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Katja |first1=Einola |last2=Violetta |first2=Khoreva |date=5 October 2022 |title=Best friend or broken tool? Exploring the co-existence of humans and artificial intelligence in the workplace ecosystem |journal=Special Issue:The Ecosystem of Work and Organization: Theoretical Frameworks and Future Directions |volume=66 |issue=1 |pages=117–135 |doi=10.1002/hrm.22147 |doi-access=free |hdl=10227/518668 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Their research shows that successful AI integration depends on human ownership and contextual understanding. They caution against blind technological optimism and stress the importance of tailoring AI use to specific workplace ecosystems. This perspective reinforces the need for inclusive design and transparent implementation strategies.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Einola |first1=Katja |last2=Khoreva |first2=Violetta |title=Best Friend or Broken Tool? Exploring the Co-existence of Humans and Artificial Intelligence in the Workplace Ecosystem |journal=Human Resource Management |volume=62 |issue=1 |pages=117–135 |year=2023 |doi=10.1002/hrm.22147|doi-access=free |hdl=10227/518668 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

==== Changes in work practices ====
{{see also|Digital divide}} 

Use of AI tools in the workplace may also be more accurately defined as "augmented intelligence" to highlight the augmentation of human intelligence with an AI tool, making specific combinations of human-and-AI action definitively important as contextual choices are made whether human or AI capacities should be put first in different circumstances.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wells |first=Joshua |last2=VanderVeen |first2=James |date=2026 |title=An Anthropological Understanding of Artificial Intelligence Transformations in Civic and Domestic Life, Labor, and Higher Education Through the Cybernetic Organism (Cyborg) Concept |url=https://www.proquest.com/openview/639ef067e3f8c2598a88bcf491d198b1 |journal=Maguare |volume=40 |issue=1 |pages=157–184 |via=ProQuest}}</ref> In some circumstances, over-reliance on AI tools may lead to [[deskilling]] of some professions.<ref name="implications" /> 

When AI becomes a substitute for traditional peer collaboration and mentorship, there is a risk of diminishing opportunities for interpersonal skill development and [[team-based learning]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Yusuf |first1=Samuel |last2=Abubakar |first2=Justina |last3=Durodola |first3=Remilekun |year=2024 |title=Impact of AI on continuous learning and skill development in the workplace: A comparative study with traditional methods |url=https://wjarr.com/content/impact-ai-continuous-learning-and-skill-development-workplace-comparative-study-traditional |journal=World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews |volume=23 |issue=2 |pages=1129–1140 |doi=10.30574/wjarr.2024.23.2.2439 |doi-access=free |access-date=26 June 2025|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Increased monitoring may lead to [[micromanagement]] and thus to stress and anxiety.<ref>{{Cite web |date=29 October 2024 |title='Why do I feel like somebody's watching me?' Workplace Surveillance Can Impact More Than Just Productivity |url=https://www.gao.gov/blog/why-do-i-feel-somebodys-watching-me-workplace-surveillance-can-impact-more-just-productivity |access-date=7 September 2025 |website=GAO}}</ref>  A perception of [[surveillance]] may also lead to stress.  Controls for these include consultation with worker groups, extensive testing, and attention to introduced bias.  [[Wearable technology|Wearable sensors]], [[activity tracker]]s, and [[augmented reality]] may also lead to stress from micromanagement, both for assembly line workers and [[gig worker]]s.  Gig workers also lack the legal protections and rights of formal workers.<ref name="benefits" />{{Rp|2–10}}

Newell & Marabelli argue that AI alters power dynamics and employee autonomy, requiring a more nuanced understanding of its social and organizational implications.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Newell |first1=Sue |last2=Marabelli |first2=Marco |title=Artificial Intelligence and the Changing Nature of Work |journal=Academy of Management Discoveries |volume=7 |issue=4 |pages=521–536 |year=2021 |doi=10.5465/amd.2019.0103 |url=https://research.vu.nl/en/publications/d627f265-b4f0-42f2-806a-f57de5947ed4 |hdl=1871.1/d627f265-b4f0-42f2-806a-f57de5947ed4 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>{{primary inline|date=May 2026}}

There is also the risk of people being forced to work at a robot's pace, or to monitor robot performance at nonstandard hours.<ref name="benefits" />{{Rp|5–7}}

A 2025 [[preprint]] paper based on users' interactions with the AI chatbot [[Microsoft Copilot]] identified forty jobs that the authors claimed had high overlaps with the capabilities of AI.<ref>{{cite arXiv|last1=Tomlinson |first1=Kiran |title=Working with AI: Measuring the Applicability of Generative AI to Occupations |date=2025 |eprint=2507.07935 |last2=Jaffe |first2=Sonia |last3=Wang |first3=Will |last4=Counts |first4=Scott |last5=Suri |first5=Siddharth |class=cs.AI }}</ref> Some media outlets used this paper to report on jobs becoming obsolete. Criticism of the paper suggesting that it had misrepresented typical workplace activities to augment AI's current performance. The historian Chris Campbell argued that the "report's methods, deliberately or otherwise, de-skill historians away from a job that requires high-level and deeply human analytical skills to one that is tasked solely with the retention and provision of knowledge. Under that flawed rubric, it is little wonder that historians have a high AI applicability score."<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Campbell |first=Chris |date=10 December 2025 |title=The Historian in the Age of AI |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S0080440125100509/type/journal_article |journal=Transactions of the Royal Historical Society |language=en |pages=1–11 |doi=10.1017/S0080440125100509 |issn=0080-4401|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==== Bias ====
{{Main|Algorithmic bias}}
Algorithms trained on past decisions may mimic undesirable human [[bias]]es, for example, past [[Employment discrimination|discriminatory hiring and firing practices]].  [[Information asymmetry]] between management and workers may lead to stress, if workers do not have access to the data or algorithms that are the basis for decision-making.<ref name="benefits" />{{Rp|3–5}}

In addition to building a model with inadvertently discriminatory features, intentional discrimination may occur through designing metrics that covertly result in discrimination through [[Correlation and dependence|correlated variables]] in a non-obvious way.<ref name="benefits" />{{Rp|12–13}}

In complex human‐machine interactions, some approaches to [[accident analysis]] may be biased to safeguard a technological system and its developers by [[Blame in organizations|assigning blame]] to the individual human operator instead.<ref name="implications" />

=== Physical ===
[[File:AGVs amarillos.jpg|alt=A yellow rectangular wheeled forklift robot in a warehouse, with stacks of boxes visible and additional similar robots visible behind it|thumb|[[Automated guided vehicle]]s are examples of [[cobot]]s currently in common use.  Use of AI to operate these robots may affect the risk of [[physical hazard]]s such as the robot or its moving parts colliding with workers.]]
[[Physical hazard]]s in the form of human–robot collisions may arise from robots using AI, especially collaborative robots ([[cobot]]s).  Cobots are intended to operate in close proximity to humans,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hubbard |first=Scott |date=21 August 2025 |title=Collaborative Robots 101: What You Need to Know About Cobots |url=https://crx.fanucamerica.com/articles/why-cobots-collaborative-robots |access-date=16 October 2025 |website=CRX Collaborative Robot |language=en-US}}</ref> which makes impossible the common hazard control of [[Workplace robotics safety|isolating the robot]] using fences or other barriers, which is widely used for traditional [[industrial robot]]s.  [[Automated guided vehicle]]s are a type of cobot that as of 2019 are in common use, often as [[forklift]]s or [[pallet jack]]s in [[warehouse]]s or factories.<ref name="risks" />{{Rp|5, 29–30}}  For cobots, sensor malfunctions or unexpected work environment conditions can lead to unpredictable robot behavior and thus to human–robot collisions.<ref name="benefits" />{{Rp|5–7}}

[[Self-driving car]]s are another example of AI-enabled robots.  In addition, the [[Human factors and ergonomics|ergonomics]] of control interfaces and human–machine interactions may give rise to hazards.<ref name="health" />

== Hazard controls ==
AI, in common with other computational technologies, requires [[Computer security|cybersecurity]] measures to stop software breaches and intrusions,<ref name="risks" />{{Rp|17}} as well as [[information privacy]] measures.<ref name="ergonomic" />  Communication and transparency with workers about data usage is a control for psychosocial hazards arising from security and privacy issues.<ref name="ergonomic" /> Proposed best practices for employer‐sponsored worker monitoring programs include using only validated sensor technologies; ensuring voluntary worker participation; ceasing data collection outside the workplace; disclosing all data uses; and ensuring secure data storage.<ref name="implications" />

For industrial cobots equipped with AI‐enabled sensors, the [[International Organization for Standardization]] (ISO) recommended: (a) safety‐related monitored stopping controls; (b) human hand guiding of the cobot; (c) speed and separation monitoring controls; and (d) power and force limitations.  Networked AI-enabled cobots may share safety improvements with each other.<ref name="implications" /> Human oversight is another general hazard control for AI.<ref name="benefits" />{{Rp|12–13}}

== Risk management ==
Both applications and hazards arising from AI can be considered as part of existing frameworks for [[Occupational risk assessment|occupational health and safety risk management]].  As with all hazards, risk identification is most effective and least costly when [[Prevention through design|done in the design phase]].<ref name="health" />

[[Workplace health surveillance]], the collection and analysis of health data on workers, is challenging for AI because labor data are often reported in aggregate and does not provide breakdowns between different types of work, and is focused on economic data such as wages and employment rates rather than skill content of jobs.  Proxies for skill content include educational requirements and classifications of routine versus non-routine, and cognitive versus physical jobs.  However, these may still not be specific enough to distinguish specific occupations that have distinct impacts from AI.  The [[United States Department of Labor]]'s [[Occupational Information Network]] is an example of a database with a detailed taxonomy of skills.  Additionally, data are often reported on a national level, while there is much geographical variation, especially between urban and rural areas.<ref name="labor" />

AI systems in the workplace raise ethical concerns related to privacy, fairness, human dignity, and transparency. According to the OECD, these risks must be addressed through robust governance frameworks and accountability mechanisms. Ethical deployment of AI requires clear policies on data usage, explainability of algorithms, and safeguards against discrimination and surveillance.<ref>{{cite web |title=Using Artificial Intelligence in the Workplace: What Are the Main Ethical Risks? |publisher=OECD |date=2022 |url=https://one.oecd.org/document/DELSA/ELSA/WD/SEM%282022%297/en/pdf |access-date=13 August 2025}}</ref>

== Employment ==
Certain digital technologies are predicted to result in job losses. Starting in the 2020s, the adoption of modern robotics has led to net employment growth.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}} However, many businesses anticipate that automation, or employing [[robot]]s would result in job losses in the future. This is especially true for companies in [[Central Europe|Central]] and Eastern Europe.<ref name="EIB2022">{{Cite book |last=EIB |url=https://www.eib.org/en/publications/digitalisation-in-europe-2021-2022 |title=Digitalisation in Europe 2021–2022: Evidence from the EIB Investment Survey |date=5 May 2022 |publisher=European Investment Bank |isbn=978-92-861-5233-7 |language=EN}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Parschau |first1=Christian |last2=Hauge |first2=Jostein |date=1 October 2020 |title=Is automation stealing manufacturing jobs? Evidence from South Africa's apparel industry |journal=Geoforum |language=en |volume=115 |pages=120–131 |doi=10.1016/j.geoforum.2020.07.002 |s2cid=224877507 |issn=0016-7185|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Genz">{{Cite web |last=Genz |first=Sabrina |date=5 May 2022 |title=The nuanced relationship between cutting-edge technologies and jobs: Evidence from Germany |url=https://www.brookings.edu/research/the-nuanced-relationship-between-cutting-edge-technologies-and-jobs/ |access-date=5 June 2022 |website=Brookings |language=en-US}}</ref> Other digital technologies, such as [[Computing platform|platforms]] or [[big data]], are projected to have a more neutral impact on employment.<ref name="EIB2022" /><ref name="Genz" /> A large number of tech workers have been laid off starting in 2023;<ref>{{cite news|url=https://npr.org/2024/01/28/1227326215/nearly-25-000-tech-workers-laid-off-in-the-first-weeks-of-2024-whats-going-on|title=Nearly 25,000 tech workers were laid off in the first weeks of 2024. Why is that?|last=Allyn|first=Bobby|date=28 January 2024|publisher=NPR|access-date=27 November 2024}}</ref> many such job cuts have been attributed to artificial intelligence.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.intelligenceinsights.net/artificial-intelligence/ai-in-jobs-workplace-the-workplace-automation/|title=AI in Jobs & Workplace – The Workplace Automation|last=Ahirwar|first=Shalley|date=3 September 2025|publisher=INTELLIGENCEINSIGHTS.NET|access-date=17 September 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://cbsnews.com/news/tech-layoffs-artificial-intelligence-ai-chatgpt|title=Tech companies are slashing thousands of jobs as they pivot toward AI|last=Cerullo|first=Megan|date=25 January 2024|publisher=CBS|access-date=27 November 2024}}</ref> Some companies have also reduced staff to fund investment in AI. In March 2026, Oracle began laying off employees, notifying many of them by early-morning email, as it redirected spending toward AI infrastructure.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Blasi |first=Weston |date=2026-04-04 |title=‘Mass layoffs by email might be the new norm’ as Oracle lays off thousands that way |url=https://www.marketwatch.com/story/fired-via-email-some-of-the-30-000-workers-cut-by-oracle-woke-up-to-a-morning-message-saying-they-were-laid-off-89a7af94 |access-date=2026-10-23 |website=MarketWatch |language=EN-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-04-01 |title=Oracle lays off up to 30,000 staff with 6am email |url=https://www.the-independent.com/tech/oracle-layoff-ai-data-centre-b2950165.html |access-date=2026-10-23 |website=The Independent |language=en}}</ref> The company later reported about 141,000 full-time employees as of 31 May 2026, down from 162,000 a year earlier.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bhaimiya |first=Sawdah |date=2026-06-23 |title=Oracle sheds 21,000 roles over the past year amid wave of AI layoffs from tech giants |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2026/06/23/oracle-ai-job-cuts-layoffs-21000.html |access-date=2026-10-23 |website=CNBC |language=en}}</ref> An August 2026 report by the [[Stanford University|Stanford]] Digital Economy Lab stated that there was no evidence of widespread, economy-wide job displacement due to AI, but found that workers aged 22 to 25 in AI-exposed occupations had an employment level 19% lower than those in fields less exposed to AI.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Orland |first=Kyle |date=2026-08-24 |title=AI is hitting entry-level jobs hardest, Stanford study finds |url=https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/08/ai-is-hitting-entry-level-jobs-hardest-stanford-study-finds/ |access-date=2026-08-28 |website=Ars Technica |language=en}}</ref>

== Standards and regulation ==
{{Main|Regulation of artificial intelligence}}

{{As of|2019}}, ISO was developing a [[Technical standard|standard]] on the use of metrics and [[Dashboard (business)|dashboards]], information displays presenting company metrics for managers, in workplaces.  The standard is planned to include guidelines for both gathering data and displaying it in a viewable and useful manner.<ref name="benefits" />{{Rp|11}}<ref>{{Cite web|last=Moore|first=Phoebe V.|date=1 April 2014|title=Questioning occupational safety and health in the age of AI|url=https://www.kan.de/en/publications/kanbrief/setting-the-course-for-work-equipment-of-the-future/questioning-occupational-safety-and-health-in-the-age-of-ai/|access-date=6 August 2020|website=Kommission Arbeitsschutz und Normung}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Standards by ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 42 – Artificial intelligence|url=https://www.iso.org/committee/6794475/x/catalogue/p/0/u/1/w/0/d/0|access-date=6 August 2020|website=[[International Organization for Standardization]]}}</ref>

In the European Union, the [[General Data Protection Regulation]], while oriented towards consumer data, is also relevant for workplace data collection.  Data subjects, including workers, have "the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing". Other relevant [[Directive (European Union)|EU directives]] include the [[Machinery Directive]] (2006/42/EC), the [[Radio Equipment Directive]] (2014/53/EU), and the [[General Product Safety Directive]] (2001/95/EC).<ref name="benefits" />{{Rp|10, 12–13}}
